analysis.one_liner: Strengthens enforcement of equal pay for women by narrowing employer defenses and banning salary-history screening.
analysis.headline: The bill won 221 House cosponsors, including one Republican, but committees never held a hearing or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Paycheck Fairness Act would make it easier for workers to win sex-based pay discrimination cases by limiting the defenses employers can raise, adding compensatory and punitive damages, and allowing class actions. It would also ban employers from demanding or relying on a job applicant's prior salary, let workers discuss their wages without retaliation, require large employers to report pay data by sex, race, and national origin, and fund salary-negotiation training and pay-gap research.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers — especially women and workers of color, who together lose an estimated tens of billions of dollars a year to pay discrimination — gain stronger legal tools: a narrower employer defense, real damages, class-action access, protection for discussing wages, and a ban on salary-history screening that locks in past underpayment. Small businesses are exempt, and federal small-business compliance help is provided.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women workers and workers of color

how_it_helps.text: An employer could only defeat a pay-discrimination claim by proving its pay difference rests on a job-related factor tied to business necessity that explains the entire differential and is not itself derived from a sex-based pay gap.

Employees who win could recover compensatory damages, and punitive damages where the employer acted with malice or reckless indifference; equal-pay claims could be maintained as class actions under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.
Employers could not fire or retaliate against workers for inquiring about, discussing, or disclosing wages, and could not require employees to sign contracts or waivers barring wage disclosure.

Employers could not seek or rely on a job applicant's wage history in hiring or setting pay (except to support a wage higher than the one offered after a voluntary disclosure), with civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation and special damages for applicants.
Employers with 100 or more workers would have to report compensation data disaggregated by sex, race, and national origin annually, so the EEOC can target investigations of pay discrimination.
The bill defines 'sex' to include pregnancy, sexual orientation, gender identity, and sex characteristics, extending equal-pay protections to those groups.

The Department of Labor would run grant programs for salary-negotiation training and conduct studies and public outreach on pay disparities, and an interagency Equal Pay Enforcement Task Force would coordinate enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — chiefly large employers — bear new liability for compensatory and punitive damages, civil penalties, mandatory annual pay-data reporting, notice-posting requirements, and litigation risk from easier class actions. Federal agencies take on new data-collection, enforcement, training, and research duties funded by unspecified appropriations.

drawbacks.text: Employers would face substantially higher litigation exposure: punitive damages, class actions, and a defense they must prove element-by-element, which business groups argued could push companies toward rigid pay formulas and settlement of weak claims.

Employers with 100 or more employees would take on annual compensation-data reporting by sex, race, and national origin, a compliance cost the bill itself acknowledges it should weigh against enforcement benefits.
The bill authorizes appropriations of 'such sums as may be necessary' for grants, studies, and an enforcement task force with no dollar cap.
The county-based definition of 'same establishment' broadens who can be compared for pay claims beyond a single workplace, which employers argued could produce misleading cross-location comparisons.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers whose pay has been depressed by discrimination or by salary-history screening, the bill's remedies are meaningful and directly targeted at documented enforcement gaps. The costs fall on employers as litigation risk, damages exposure, and reporting paperwork, and the open-ended appropriations deserve scrutiny; the small-business exemption and required compliance assistance soften the burden on the smallest firms. On balance the bill's benefits to workers clearly outweigh its compliance costs, though the litigation expansion is the strongest good-faith objection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever held a hearing or markup on it, so it died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Paycheck Fairness Act in the House on March 10, 2023, with 221 original cosponsors.

The bill was referred to the Committee on Education and the Workforce and in addition to the Committee on Oversight and Accountability, in each case for consideration of provisions within their jurisdiction.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history for the remainder of the 118th Congress.

The bill attracted 221 cosponsors, 220 Democrats and 1 Republican (Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick), a level of support well short of what would be needed to force action but substantial for a bill that never advanced.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off because the bill died: they avoided expanded liability for compensatory and punitive damages, class-action exposure, a salary-history ban, and mandatory pay-data reporting. The bill's cosponsors, and the workers it aimed to protect, are left with the existing equal-pay enforcement system.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided new pay-bias liability

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Paycheck Fairness Act and recruited more than 200 House cosponsors.

for.name: 220 House Democratic cosponsors, including House leaders Jeffries, Pelosi, Hoyer, and Clyburn
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

for.name: Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: The only Republican cosponsor of the bill.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral (Republican majority in the 118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or report — for the entire Congress.

against.name: House Oversight and Accountability Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the provisions within its jurisdiction.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor and committee calendars
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor consideration; with committee chairs in the majority declining to act, no path to a vote existed.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was almost entirely Democratic — 220 Democrats to 1 Republican — and no vote was ever held, so the bill's fate was decided by which party controlled the House committees rather than by a recorded division.

industries.industry: Large employers (businesses with 100 or more employees)
industries.note: They would face compensatory and punitive damages, class-action exposure, annual pay-data reporting by sex, race, and national origin, and a ban on using salary history in hiring. The bill's failure leaves them free of these costs, while workers keep today's weaker equal-pay remedies.

The bill exempts small enterprises to the same extent they are exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act and requires federal compliance-assistance materials for them, but those below the FLSA thresholds would remain outside its protections too.

industries.industry: Employment litigation and compliance industries (HR consulting, EEO plaintiffs' bar)
industries.note: Expanded damages, class actions, mandatory reporting, and new compliance notices would create work for employment lawyers, HR compliance vendors, and EEO data-reporting services if the bill passed.

industries.industry: Federal enforcement agencies (EEOC, DOL's OFCCP, Bureau of Labor Statistics)
industries.note: The bill gives the EEOC and Labor Department new enforcement authority, pay-data collection mandates, training duties, and research programs, funded by open-ended appropriations.
